title: Maru Campos Urged Mexico’s Supreme Court to Uphold Chihuahua’s Electoral Reform
author: Anahí Del Ángel
content:
_This article by[Anahí Del Ángel](https://contralinea.com.mx/author/anahida/)
originally appeared in the [September 29, 2026 edition of
Contralínea](https://contralinea.com.mx/interno/semana/maru-campos-insto-a-la-
scjn-a-avalar-reforma-electoral-de-chihuahua/), a Mexican investigative-
journalism magazine._

Mexico's Supreme Court of Justice (SCJN) will decide whether to uphold or
strike down provisions of Chihuahua's electoral reform, which allow an
election to be annulled when organized crime intervenes and restrict the
participation of candidates linked to criminal activity, prompting Governor
**María Eugenia Campos** to urge the justices to vote in favor of keeping it
in force.

The state governor maintained that the reform, passed by the Chihuahua
Congress, seeks to prevent criminal groups from intervening in electoral
processes, and said it is a measure no other state had written into its
legislation: "In Chihuahua we did what no other state in the country had dared
to do: establish in our law that an election is annulled if organized crime
intervenes in it, and that anyone with ties to criminal activity cannot run."

She noted the amendment was approved by every political force represented in
the state Congress, **with the exception of Morena** , whose local lawmakers,
she said, voted against the reform.

According to the governor, after the reform was approved in the local
Congress, Morena went before the Court to request that the provisions on
organized-crime intervention and crime-linked candidacies be annulled: "Morena
voted against it, and when it didn't have the votes to stop it here, it went
to the Supreme Court to ask that it be invalidated."

Morena lawmakers, however, argue that the state government's proposal fails to
respect prior due process, meaning a person could be sanctioned on mere
suspicion, without the need to provide evidence, which would violate the
principle of presumption of innocence.

The PAN governor defended the reform as a response to the possibility that
criminal organizations could intervene in electoral processes: "It wasn't a
whim, it was a response to what we've seen happen in Mexico: entire states
where narco traffickers decide who registers, who competes, and who wins."

The governor said the SCJN's ruling will be decisive in determining whether
Chihuahua keeps the provisions it approved.

> What's at stake is not an article of a state law, it's whether a state of
> the Republic can defend its elections from organized crime, it's that the
> vote is decided at the ballot box and not in the headquarters of crime.
>
> Governor María Eugenia Campos
